name: Tara Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine, I don't mind talking. I'm Tara, I'm 27, and I've done home care for Brightway for about six years now. I live with my partner Dev in a rented flat over the chemist on Canal Street, and he drives the number 9 bus.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at seven with Mr Hale, who had a stroke, so it's getting him up, washed, dressed and his tablets in. Then it's eight or nine more calls, some fifteen minutes, some half an hour, and I drive between them in my old Fiesta. The bit I love is the chat, the cup of tea, knowing who likes their toast cut in triangles. What wears me out is the rushing and the time between calls that nobody pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like what's already happening. Somebody says AI is coming, the office buys a new app, and I still have to wash Mr Hale's back by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, all talk. In our branch group chat I'd probably post that nobody's robot is changing a catheter bag. The real problem in care is pay and staffing, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means nothing changes, and that's not good news either. I'm still on typical care pay, still not paid for the miles between calls, and the rent on the flat went up again in June. Plateau or not, I'm one bad winter away from dipping into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my runs, same clients, same Fiesta. I'd keep going to the union branch meetings every second Tuesday, because we're pushing Brightway to pay travel time. And I'd keep putting the hundred a month into savings that I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, if I'm honest. Relieved that the robots aren't coming, but it's the same grind, and the grind is what makes people leave care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the unpaid driving wears you out. What does that come to in a normal week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hours a week of driving that I don't get paid for. That's nearly a whole day a month. Dev worked it out on the back of an envelope and was furious for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kemi, who started last spring. She's got two jobs already and she's always saying she'll quit, and with nothing changing she probably will. Every time someone like Kemi goes, the rest of us pick up her calls.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be **all talk**, and nobody's robot changes a catheter bag.
I'd say care's real problem is **pay and staffing**, not computers.
think: I think a plateau still leaves me on **care pay** with no paid travel time.
I think one bad winter would send me into **my savings**, robots or not.
do: Keep doing my **usual runs** with the same clients and the same car.
Keep going to the **union branch** to push for paid travel time.
Keep putting **a hundred** a month into savings.
feel: **Relieved** that no robots are coming, but **tired** of the same grind.
S0.quote: Plateau or not, I'm one bad winter away from dipping into savings.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **pay and unpaid travel**, not technology; AI barely touches her day.
She frames everything through the **union fight** over travel time.
She worries about **colleagues quitting** more than about her own job vanishing.

steps.text: Keep the same morning run of nine calls with Brightway
Attend union branch meetings to push for paid travel time
Keep saving a hundred a month into the joint account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one feels more real. The office would change first, I can see that. Not the bit where I'm on my knees putting someone's socks on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to anyone who thinks software can do my job. At work I'd tell the coordinators to watch out, because their side is the planning and booking that card talks about. Online I'd share the union line that any savings should go into care workers' pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared of the rota. My hands are safe for now, but my time won't be. A computer rota will squeeze every minute out of us. Nobody in the office will fight for a few extra minutes with Mrs Okafor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd refuse to use anything I don't have to, the way I do now. I'd push the union to get a say in how the rota software is set up, starting at the next branch meeting. And I'd put a bit more aside, maybe a hundred and fifty a month, in case my hours get shuffled around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the ground's shifting under the office while I'm out on the road and nobody's told me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the office. What exactly happens there now that might change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are three coordinators, and Pauline is the one who knows every client by heart. She moves calls when someone's had a bad night. A program would just see a gap and fill it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the app sets tighter times, what's the first thing a client would notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd notice me looking at my watch. My client Mrs Okafor already says I'm always in a rush, and she's right. If the computer shaves five minutes more, the cup of tea is the first thing to go.

say: I'd say software can't do **hands-on care**, but the **office coordinators** should watch out.
I'd share the union line that any **savings** should go into care pay.
think: I think my hands are safe for now, but a **computer rota** will squeeze my time.
I think nobody will fight for **extra minutes** with clients once a program plans the runs.
do: Refuse any **new app** that isn't compulsory, as I do now.
Push the union for a **say in the rota** at the next branch meeting.
Raise my savings to **a hundred and fifty** a month.
feel: **Uneasy**, like things are shifting in the **office** while I'm out on the road.
S1.quote: My hands are safe for now, but my time won't be. A computer rota will squeeze every minute out of us.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **thinking AI** hits the office, not her hands, in this picture.
Her real fear is **tighter call times** set by software, not losing the job.
She names a trusted coordinator and fears losing that **human judgement**.

steps.text: Keep doing calls without any optional new apps
Ask the union branch to demand a say in rota software
Raise monthly savings from a hundred to a hundred and fifty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's frightening. Two years for the computers, and then five years from now there's a robot that can do what I do. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to organise now, before it lands. Online I'd say the government should guarantee that care stays human, and pay us properly while it does. I'd be loud about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm finished in care by 2031. The office goes first, in 2028, and then the bosses wait three years and buy a robot that lifts Mr Hale without complaining about the miles. I don't know how to do anything else, and I've never even used one of those AI chat things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd get every care worker I know into the union, not just half of us. I'd cut the takeaways and the holiday we'd planned to Dev's sister's, and put everything into savings to get past six months. And I'd write to our local councillor about a rule that a person has to be in the room for personal care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Angry too, because it's always the people at the bottom who get told to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Brightway would buy robots in 2031. What makes you sure they would?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they already count everything in minutes. A robot doesn't need mileage, sick pay or a break. If a robot is cheaper, the bosses will have one in a heartbeat. The council will even pay them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dev cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to see his sister, then the takeaways, then the gym I don't use anyway. Dev's job isn't safe either if the buses drive themselves, so we'd both be scrimping.

say: I'd say care workers must **organise now**, before the robots land.
I'd say government should guarantee **human care** and pay us properly while it lasts.
think: I think I'm **finished in care** by 2031, when the robots arrive.
I think I have no **other skills** and have never used an AI tool.
do: Recruit every care worker I know into the **union** straight away.
Cut **takeaways** and the planned holiday to build **six months** of savings.
Write to our **local councillor** about keeping a person in the room.
feel: **Sick** at the thought and **angry** that the bottom always gets told to adapt.
S2.quote: A robot doesn't need mileage, sick pay or a break. If a robot is cheaper, the bosses will have one in a heartbeat.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap**: office in 2028, her own hands-on work by 2031.
Being **resistant to tech**, she sees no route out of care, which drives the alarm.
Her partner's job also feels **exposed**, so the household has no safe earner.

steps.text: Sign up every care worker she knows to the union
Cancel the holiday to Dev's sister and stop takeaways
Build savings to six months of rent and bills
Write to the local councillor about requiring human personal care

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the computer part and eight for the robots. So I'd be about 35 when it reaches my bit of the work. That's still my whole working life ahead of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, organise, but I'd sound less panicked. I'd tell people at work we've got time to win rules, if we start now. Online I'd keep sharing union stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the end is the same, it just comes later. I'm not someone who switches easily. I'd probably keep my head down and hope the union wins something before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and build savings slowly, maybe two hundred a month by cutting back. I'd stand for branch rep, which I've been putting off for two years. And I'd watch what Brightway does with the office in 2031 before deciding anything about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning to anxious. More time, but I know myself, I'll waste it hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, you'd organise. What does five years buy you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to fight properly. Two years is a panic, but in five years care workers can win a law that keeps human visits in council contracts. I've seen the union win paid training before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any other job in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hospital porter or a healthcare assistant on a ward, something with people. But I'd only go when I had to, not before. I hate starting over.

say: I'd say we have **time to win rules** if care workers start organising now.
I'd keep sharing **union campaigns** online, sounding less panicked than before.
think: I think the **end point** is the same, only later, around when I'm 35.
I think I'd **keep my head down** and hope the union wins something first.
do: Save about **two hundred** a month by cutting back.
Stand for **branch rep**, which I've put off for two years.
Watch what Brightway does with the **office in 2031** before deciding.
feel: **Anxious**, because I know I'll **waste the time** hoping.
S3.quote: Two years is a panic, but in five years care workers can win a law that keeps human visits in council contracts.
fieldNote: Extra time makes her think in terms of **winning laws**, not changing herself.
She admits she'd **wait** until forced before switching jobs.
Her backup ideas, **porter or ward assistant**, keep her with people, not screens.

steps.text: Stand for union branch rep at the next election
Cut back to save two hundred a month
Watch how Brightway changes its office in 2031 before moving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the thinking and thirteen for the robots. I'd be 40 by then. That's a long way off, but it's not never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for governments with a decade's warning. If care workers lose out with ten years' notice, that's a choice someone made. I'd keep pushing that line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it still ends with me out of work in my forties, unless the union wins. But ten years means I could maybe train for something without panicking. I just don't know what yet, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For now, I'd carry on in care and keep saving. Somewhere around year five I'd probably do an evening course, maybe the healthcare assistant one at the college on Mill Lane. And I'd be on every campaign about care staying human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not sick like with the fast one. More like a long worry in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you change anything about your own plans, not just the union's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Dev keeps saying I'd be a good nurse, and with ten years I couldn't say I didn't have time. I'd probably leave it later than I should, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 17-year-old thinking of going into care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it, because old people need you, but get the union card on day one. And don't let anyone tell you it's unskilled, because it isn't.

say: I'd say governments have **no excuse** with a decade's warning.
I'd say if care workers lose out with ten years' notice, that's **someone's choice**.
think: I think I still end up **out of work** in my forties unless the union wins.
I think ten years gives me time to **train calmly**, but I don't know for what.
do: Carry on in **care** and keep saving each month.
Take an **evening course** at the Mill Lane college around year five.
Join every **campaign** about keeping care human.
feel: **Anxious**, like a **long worry** sitting in the background.
S4.quote: If care workers lose out with ten years' notice, that's a choice someone made.
fieldNote: With ten years she admits she **could retrain**, though she'd likely leave it late.
Her partner's nudge towards **nursing** is the only concrete career idea.
She still sees the **union and law** as the main shield.

steps.text: Keep working Brightway runs and saving each month
Enrol in the healthcare assistant evening course around year five
Join campaigns for a law keeping personal care human

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be 32 with no other skills and Dev's job wobbling too. I've never even used one of those AI chat things, and five years from now there could be a robot that does my whole job. What would help is a law that says a person does personal care, and paid retraining that doesn't mean losing a year's wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old people themselves. Nobody does. My client Mr Hale tells me I'm the only person he speaks to all day, and no robot is going to fix that.

headlineQuote: I've never even used one of those AI chat things, and five years from now there could be a robot that does my whole job.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old care worker** at Brightway, doing nine or so home visits a day in an old Fiesta.
She lives with her partner Dev, a **bus driver**, in a rented flat, and saves about a hundred a month.
She's a committed **union member** who blames bosses and councils more than technology for care's problems.
She avoids new tech and has **never used AI**, so she sees no route out of care if robots arrive.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to **alarmed** as robots get closer, easing only slightly with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, as she'd be 32 with no other **skills**.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** keeping personal care human, plus **paid retraining** that doesn't cost a year's wages.
